world.org_type: nonprofit regional health system with four hospitals and an employed medical group, replacing commercial occurrence professional liability policies with a self-insured claims-made trust

driver: A cover whose first window sees only the events reported soon after they occur is priced on a history in which only some units ran the process that produces those quick, cheap reports, while every unit runs it from the window's start; the window's cost is carried almost entirely by the quick events that only the process's units show, so the history pooled across every unit about halves it, and the process's effect read over a full period of development, where it makes the units look cheaper, points the wrong way; the window is costed at each point of its exposure on the experience of the units that already ran the process, one rate for every unit.
driver_concrete: From each Transition Date every entity's patients can request compensation through the Early Resolution Program, which until now served only Tolliver Falls and Alderwick while Stoneleigh adjusted the medical group's and Brennick's claims; a first claims-made window catches mostly those quick requests, so the System's pooled 2017 to 2024 experience, diluted by the medical group's and Brennick's exposure without the Program, prices the window at about half, and the Program hospitals' lower full-year cost per FTE-year would cut it further; the 2027 cost is each entity's window costed day by day on Tolliver Falls' and Alderwick's class experience, one rate per class for all four entities.
stump: A strong solver collapses the register to one Claim per incident, trends it, and costs each entity's claims-made window day by day, every experience Claim counted where its own delay brings it in by 31 December 2027, on the System's pooled 2017 to 2024 experience by specialty class, and files $312,000; the step that lands it there is pricing the window on experience in which the medical group's and Brennick's patients had no Early Resolution Program, when from each Transition Date every entity's patients can come through it (trust agreement 5.2) and the window's cost is almost all the quick requests only Tolliver Falls' and Alderwick's experience shows: costed on those hospitals' experience the contribution is $587,000.
analyst_test: a strong analyst who dedupes the register, reads the trust agreement and the funding policy and costs each entity's claims-made window claim by claim and day by day still prices it on the System's pooled experience by class and files $312,000 (adjusting for the Program by its full-year cost relativity, $273,000), because the medical group's and Brennick's experience holds no early requests while every entity's patients can make them from its Transition Date; costed on the Program hospitals' experience the window is $587,000.
domain_test: the deciding quantity is the expected cost of the claims first made in a claims-made trust's opening window, an exposure-weighted, report-lag-truncated experience rate by specialty class that a professional liability actuary must base on experience generated under the claims handling the trust will run (the early resolution program every entity joins), the ratemaking adjustment for a change in claims practice; with another field's nouns the retroactive dates, report lags, early-offer requests and specialty classes have nothing to attach to.

differentiation.task102: task102 moves payments across a period boundary by a business-day release rule; here nothing moves across a boundary: a claims-made window keeps only the claims made soon after their incident, which are the cheap early-resolution ones, so the cost is the exposure at each point of each entity's months of cover times the cost of past claims made within the time then left.
differentiation.task501: task501 v3 sized a buffer on a cumulative path's furthest overrun, and v4 rebuilds a contact matrix from the diaries kept in one season's regime; here the regime is not a season of the same units but a claims process some units ran and every unit runs from the window's start, its effect reverses with the horizon (cheaper over full development, dearer in a first claims-made window), and the window is a lag-truncated cost per day of exposure carried to units that never ran the process.
differentiation.task136: task136 carries an intervention's increment to a new site as a multiple of the site's own recent rate; here no unit's own rate is scaled: the units that never ran the claims process have no early requests to scale, the trust rates every unit alike, and the window is costed on the process units' class experience, a lag-truncated cost per day of exposure.
differentiation.task124: task124 takes the unexamined units' rate from the exhaustively examined groups less the outcomes already found; here nothing is netted and no unit is unexamined: every claim of the experience is recorded, the medical group's and Brennick's simply arose under another claims process, and the first claims-made window sees only the quick claims the Program produces.
differentiation.task98: task98 v6 counts units leaving a class when a scheduled improvement lifts some over a score threshold, the step recovered from improved and unimproved twins; here nothing crosses a threshold and no twin step is recovered: the expected cost of a claims-made opening window is priced on the experience of the units that already ran the claims process every unit runs from the window's start, a lag-truncated cost per day of exposure at one rate for every unit.

lineage.driver: The committed set is read off holdings on a future effective date built forward from a past snapshot of filed returns; the forward roll, with a third party's takeovers of scheduled transfers completed on the fixed interval its settled cases show, reproduces both closed controls because every holder enrolled by the snapshot had filed, but the holder population on the effective date also takes in holders enrolled after the snapshot who have not filed yet, whose units are recoverable only by grouping the transfer extract on the buyer, so a unit the roll leaves under the threshold is over it.

lineage.driver: Members of a closed group leave only when a rationed supply reaches them, and the supply is handed out across a wider list in a filed priority order within each size class, so how many remain at a later date is each member's rank inside its class against the cumulative planned supply, and neither a leaving rate nor a survival curve read off history, which both average over whatever list length the past happened to have, gives it.

lineage.fate: rejected at the clone pre-flight (Template, Track B, against task73 world ten)
lineage.driver: A waiting list is split into classes by an attribute the governing rule works out on the day from each member's composition, while the case record keeps that attribute as last assessed; a run-off forecast against a planned supply has to recompute every member's class on each allocation day, because members age across the rule's thresholds and a record assessed years earlier holds the longest-waiting members in classes they have already left.

lineage.driver: A group chosen for an extreme value of a noisy outcome in one period is forecast for the next period by carrying its own chosen-period value forward with trend, when the outcome regresses toward the mean; the forecast that holds is the next-period experience of a group chosen the same way one period earlier, which the record contains untreated, cell by cell.

lineage.fate: shipped 2026-10-12 (judge DETERMINISTIC, APPROVE); weak per the 10/10 audit of 2026-10-14: the decisive step (cost-weighted report-lag truncation, per day) was visible and near a reflex for a strong model, the funding policy narrowed the method to it, and both asks were cracked unaided; round 2 keeps the window as a lower rung and moves the decisive step to the claims process the window runs under
lineage.driver: A cover that pays only for events that both occur and are first reported inside its own window is costed from a full period's cost per unit of exposure, when inside a short window only the events reported soon after they occur can count and here those are the cheap ones; the expected cost is the exposure at each point of the window times the cost of past events reported within the time then left, which neither a full period's cost, its prorated share nor the share of events reported within a year at the average cost gives.
